blocks.text: A skin stapler is a handheld medical device used to approximate the edges of a skin wound or surgical incision using sterile metal staples, usually made of stainless steel or titanium.
It is commonly used for rapid closure of suitable surgical wounds, particularly longer incisions where efficient skin approximation is desirable.
Key OSCE distinction: A skin stapler closes the skin; it does not usually close the deeper subcutaneous tissue, fascia or internal organs. Those layers may require separate closure.
Identification: Disposable surgical skin stapler.
Characteristic features

items.text: Handheld, pistol-shaped or pen-like body.
Handle or trigger mechanism.
Cartridge containing preloaded metal staples.
Distal nose or applicator tip.
Firing mechanism that forms a staple across approximated skin edges.
Often has a transparent or visible staple window, depending on design.

blocks.text: Most commonly encountered skin staplers are single-use devices. Reusable or specialised systems may differ.

blocks.text: 1. Disposable skin stapler
Preloaded, usually sterile, and discarded after use according to the manufacturer's instructions. Common in routine surgical wound closure.
2. Skin staple remover
A separate instrument used to deform and extract staples during wound review. It is not the device used to insert staples.
Staples vary in width, leg length, material and intended wound application. The correct staple size depends on the device, skin thickness and wound characteristics.
A common skin staple is designed to form a bridge across the skin edges, with its legs entering the skin and bending inward during firing.
The skin stapler approximates the wound edges mechanically.

items.text: The wound edges are brought into alignment manually or with suitable forceps.
The applicator is positioned perpendicular to the skin, according to the device instructions.
The trigger is activated.
A metal staple penetrates the skin on either side of the incision.
The staple-forming mechanism bends the legs inward, holding the wound edges together.
The operator checks the approximation, spacing and haemostasis before placing additional staples.

blocks.text: The objective is accurate skin-edge eversion or approximation without excessive tension, crushing or strangulation of the tissue.

blocks.title: Skin staplers are commonly used for:

items.text: Closure of suitable abdominal surgical incisions.
Closure of selected orthopaedic surgical wounds.
Closure of scalp lacerations.
Closure of suitable trunk and extremity wounds.
Rapid closure of selected long surgical incisions.
Wounds where cosmetic requirements and anatomical location make stapling appropriate.

blocks.text: They are generally most useful for wounds with accessible edges that can be adequately approximated without excessive tension.

rows: Wound under excessive tension
Address tension and consider deeper sutures or another closure strategy.
Poorly approximated wound edges
Reposition and align the edges before closure.
Deep wound with unclosed underlying layers
Assess whether deeper closure is required first.
Contaminated or infected wound
Consider irrigation, debridement and delayed or alternative closure when indicated.
Delicate cosmetic areas, such as the face
Fine sutures may offer a better cosmetic result, depending on the wound.
Wound with suspected underlying structural injury
Assess and treat deeper injury before closing the skin.
Fragile skin or poor tissue integrity
Staples may tear or inadequately secure the edges; individualise the closure method.

blocks.text: These are clinical considerations rather than universal absolute contraindications. Wound management depends on the site, contamination, timing, patient factors and available expertise.

blocks.text: A. Wound dehiscence
The wound edges separate because of inadequate approximation, excessive tension, infection or impaired healing.
B. Infection
May occur because of wound contamination, inadequate wound preparation or other patient and procedural factors.
C. Skin-edge ischaemia or necrosis
Excessive tissue compression or poorly placed staples may compromise local perfusion.
D. Bleeding or haematoma
Inadequate haemostasis before closure may allow blood to accumulate beneath the wound.
E. Cosmetic problems and staple marks
Poor spacing, excessive tension, prolonged retention or inappropriate closure technique may cause prominent scars or local skin marks.
Other complications include pain, accidental skin injury, retained staples and difficulty removing staples that are bent or embedded.
The following is a supervised clinical skills framework.

items.text: Preparation: Explain the procedure, obtain consent, check allergies and relevant clinical factors, prepare the wound and maintain aseptic technique.
Wound assessment: Check the depth, contamination, haemostasis, tissue viability and whether deeper layers require closure.
Approximation: Align the wound edges accurately, using forceps or assistance where necessary.
Positioning: Place the applicator over the wound according to the manufacturer's instructions, ensuring that the intended tissue is correctly positioned.
Stapling: Activate the trigger in a controlled manner, releasing each staple and checking the approximation as you proceed.
Spacing: Place staples at suitable intervals for the wound and device, avoiding excessive tension or gaps.
Final inspection: Confirm that the edges are approximated, haemostasis is satisfactory and no staple is excessively tight or poorly formed.
Aftercare: Apply an appropriate dressing, provide wound-care advice and arrange review and removal when indicated.
Documentation: Record the wound assessment, closure method, complications, dressing and follow-up plan.

Conventional skin staples are removed using a dedicated staple remover when the wound has healed sufficiently and removal is clinically appropriate.
The general principle is to engage the staple with the remover, deform it to release the legs from the skin and withdraw it gently without damaging the wound.

items.text: Inspect the wound before removal.
Check for infection, separation, poor healing or excessive tension.
Follow the prescribed removal schedule and local protocol.
If the wound appears unstable, reassess before removing all staples.
Removal timing varies by anatomical site, healing, patient factors and the clinician's plan.
Apply appropriate wound support after removal if indicated.

blocks.text: Q1. Identify the instrument.
This is a surgical skin stapler, used to approximate the edges of suitable skin wounds or surgical incisions using metal staples.
Q2. What is the difference between a surgical stapler and a skin stapler?
A surgical stapler is designed for internal tissue closure, division or anastomosis, while a skin stapler is designed primarily for external skin closure.
Q3. What instrument is used to remove skin staples?
A dedicated surgical staple remover.
Q4. Why must the wound edges be approximated before stapling?
Accurate approximation promotes appropriate healing and reduces gaps, malalignment and excessive tension.
Q5. What are the complications of skin stapling?
Wound dehiscence, infection, bleeding, skin-edge ischaemia, scarring, pain and retained staples.
Q6. What factors determine when staples should be removed?
The anatomical site, wound healing, tension, patient-specific risk factors and the clinician's assessment.
Q7. Why might sutures be preferred to staples?
Sutures may provide better precision or cosmetic results in selected wounds, allow layered closure and accommodate irregular wound geometry more effectively.

blocks.text: “This is a surgical skin stapler, a handheld device used to approximate the edges of suitable skin wounds and surgical incisions. It consists of a handle, trigger, applicator tip and cartridge containing metal staples. When activated, it deploys and forms a staple that holds the skin edges together. It is commonly used for selected abdominal, orthopaedic and scalp wounds. Advantages include rapid application and consistent closure. Complications include wound infection, dehiscence, poor cosmetic outcome and skin-edge ischaemia. Conventional removable staples are removed using a dedicated staple remover when healing is adequate.”
